main.summary: World War I began on 28 July 1914 and continued until 11 November 1918, drawing the Allies and Central Powers into a global conflict.

cards.heading: World War I
cards.text: World War I began on 28 July 1914 and continued until 11 November 1918, drawing the Allies and Central Powers into a global conflict. Imperial rivalries, military alliances and an arms race had sharpened tensions across Europe. The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo brought them to a crisis: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, and Russia mobilised in Serbia's defence. Machine guns, artillery, aircraft, chemical weapons and tanks transformed the fighting. Between 15 and 22 million people died, including victims of war crimes and genocides.

main.title: Einstein presents general relativity
main.summary: Albert Einstein presented the field equations of general relativity in 1915, connecting gravity to the shape of spacetime.

cards.heading: Einstein presents general relativity
cards.text: Albert Einstein presented the field equations of general relativity in 1915, connecting gravity to the shape of spacetime. Matter and radiation curve space and time; that curvature guides how objects move. The theory extended special relativity and refined Newton's account of gravitation, bringing gravity into a unified geometric description. Einstein published a detailed account in May 1916. Newton's familiar predictions remain useful around stationary masses where spacetime is nearly flat, while general relativity describes effects that the earlier theory could not explain.

main.title: Russian Revolution
main.summary: Russia's revolution began in February 1917 amid military defeats and food shortages during World War I.

cards.heading: Russian Revolution
cards.text: Russia's revolution began in February 1917 amid military defeats and food shortages during World War I. Falling morale in the army and unrest at home undermined the monarchy. Tsar Nicholas II abdicated on 15 March, and a provisional government took office under the Duma. In Petrograd, local people also formed soviet councils, seeking influence over government and control of the militias. During the October Revolution, the Bolsheviks seized power from the provisional government. The two revolutions ended the monarchy and established a socialist government, followed by civil war.

main.title: Spanish flu
main.summary: An influenza pandemic spread around the world from 1918 to 1920, infecting an estimated 500 million people, nearly a third of the population.

cards.heading: Spanish flu
cards.text: An influenza pandemic spread around the world from 1918 to 1920, infecting an estimated 500 million people, nearly a third of the population. Caused by an H1N1 influenza A virus, it killed at least 17 million, with many estimates reaching 50 million or more. Wartime censorship restricted reporting in countries fighting World War I. Newspapers in neutral Spain could report freely, creating the impression that Spain was the outbreak's centre and giving rise to the name Spanish flu. Its geographical origin remains uncertain.

main.title: Treaty of Versailles
main.summary: The Treaty of Versailles was a peace treaty signed on 28 June 1919.

cards.heading: Treaty of Versailles
cards.text:
The Treaty of Versailles was a peace treaty signed on 28 June 1919. As the most important treaty of World War I, it ended the state of war between Germany and most of the Allied Powers. It was signed in the Palace of Versailles, exactly five years after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the proximate cause of the war. The other Central Powers on the German side signed separate treaties. Although the armistice of 11 November 1918 ended the actual fighting, and agreed certain principles and conditions including the payment of reparations, it took six months of Allied negotiations at the Paris Peace Conference to conclude the peace treaty. Germany was not allowed to participate in the negotiations before signing the treaty. 

The treaty required Germany to disarm, make territorial concessions, extradite alleged war criminals, agree to Kaiser Wilhelm being put on trial, recognise the independence of states whose territory had previously been part of the German Empire, and pay reparations to the Entente powers.

main.title: League of Nations
main.summary: The League of Nations began on 10 January 1920, following the peace settlement that ended World War I.

cards.heading: League of Nations
cards.text: The League of Nations began on 10 January 1920, following the peace settlement that ended World War I. Its Covenant proposed collective security, disarmament and negotiation as ways to prevent another war. International cooperation also covered working conditions, health, trafficking, prisoners of war and minority protection. These responsibilities gave the organisation a role beyond settling disputes between governments. The League ceased operations in April 1946, after World War II; many of its components passed to the newly created United Nations.

main.title: Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution
main.summary: Adopted in August 1920, the Nineteenth Amendment prohibited denying US citizens the vote on the basis of sex.

cards.heading: Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution
cards.text: The Nineteenth Amendment (Amendment XIX) to the United States Constitution prohibits the United States and its states from denying the right to vote to citizens of the United States on the basis of sex, in effect recognizing the right of women to vote. The amendment was the culmination of a decades-long movement for women's suffrage in the United States, at both the state and national levels, and was part of the worldwide movement towards women's suffrage and part of the wider women's rights movement. The first women's suffrage amendment was introduced in Congress in 1878. However, a suffrage amendment did not pass the House of Representatives until May 21, 1919, which was quickly followed by the Senate, on June 4, 1919. It was then submitted to the states for ratification, achieving the requisite 36 ratifications to secure adoption, and thereby went into effect, on August 18, 1920. The Nineteenth Amendment's adoption was certified on August 26, 1920.

main.title: Federico Fellini
main.subtitle: Born in Rimini: a filmmaker of memory, spectacle and dreams
main.summary: Federico Fellini was born in Rimini on 20 January 1920. His films would repeatedly return to provincial life, performance and the uncertain border between memory and invention. He began as a caricaturist and writer before directing, developing an eye for faces and behaviour that remained visible in his crowded streets, circuses and film studios.

cards.heading: Born in Rimini
cards.text: Federico Fellini was born in Rimini on 20 January 1920. His films would repeatedly return to provincial life, performance and the uncertain border between memory and invention. He began as a caricaturist and writer before directing, developing an eye for faces and behaviour that remained visible in his crowded streets, circuses and film studios.

cards.heading: From drawings to films
cards.text: After moving to Rome, Fellini worked for the satirical magazine Marc'Aurelio and wrote for radio and variety performers. Radio brought him together with Giulietta Masina, whom he married in 1943. His screenwriting work with Roberto Rossellini included Rome, Open City and Paisan. When he became a director, that experience of street life met a growing interest in spectacle. Masina's performances in La strada and Nights of Cabiria gave two of his films their emotional centre.

cards.heading: Finding a personal cinema
cards.text: La dolce vita follows a journalist through Rome's public celebrations and private disappointments. In 8½, a director's stalled production becomes a way of entering his memories and fantasies; Amarcord reshapes a provincial childhood into an ensemble of rituals and stories. Working with collaborators such as composer Nino Rota, Fellini made these imagined worlds distinct in their sound and movement. Four of his films won the foreign-language Oscar, and the Academy honoured his career in 1993.

main.title: R.U.R.
main.summary: Karel Čapek's play R.U.R. premiered in January 1921 and introduced the word robot into science fiction.

cards.heading: R.U.R.
cards.text:
R.U.R. is a 1920 science fiction play by the Czech writer Karel Čapek. "R.U.R." stands for Rossumovi Univerzální Roboti (Rossum's Universal Robots, a phrase that has been used as a subtitle in English versions).

The play had its world premiere on 2 January 1921 in Hradec Králové. It introduced the word "robot" to the English language and to science fiction as a whole. R.U.R. became influential soon after its publication.

By 1923, it had been translated into thirty languages. R.U.R. was successful in its time in Europe and North America. Čapek later took a different approach to the same theme in his 1936 novel War with the Newts, in which non-humans become a servant-class in human society.

main.title: The BBC: broadcasting begins
main.summary: The British Broadcasting Company was established in 1922, beginning the organisation that became the British Broadcasting Corporation on 1 January 1927.

cards.heading: The BBC: broadcasting begins
cards.text: The British Broadcasting Company was established in 1922, beginning the organisation that became the British Broadcasting Corporation on 1 January 1927. Operating under a royal charter, the BBC developed a public-service model for radio and later television. An annual licence fee became its principal source of funding, supporting services across Britain's nations and regions. Its international work expanded with the BBC Empire Service in 1932, later known as the World Service. The company's foundation marks the start of an enduring British broadcasting institution.
